title: Financial Sentiment Analysis: The Effect of Annotation Agreement on Classification Performance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat University - Department of Computer Engineering

detail.title: Financial Sentiment Analysis: The Effect of Annotation Agreement on Classification Performance
detail.abstract: Annotation agreement is an important indicator of annotation quality in supervised text classification; however, its effect on financial sentiment classification has received limited attention. This study investigates the influence of annotation agreement on classification performance using the Financial PhraseBank dataset. Three mutually exclusive datasets representing high, medium, and low agreement annotations were constructed to eliminate duplicated instances across agreement levels. Nine within-level and cross-level experimental settings were evaluated using two preprocessing configurations, TF-IDF unigram features, and eight traditional machine learning classifiers. Experimental results showed that classification performance consistently decreased as annotation agreement declined. Models evaluated on higher-agreement test datasets consistently achieved better performance than those evaluated on lower-agreement datasets, regardless of the annotation agreement level of the training data. Linear SVM and SGD (Hinge) achieved the highest Macro-F1 scores across most experimental settings, whereas lemmatization provided only limited and inconsistent improvements. These findings demonstrate that annotation agreement is an important characteristic of annotated datasets and should be explicitly considered when constructing benchmark datasets, evaluating financial sentiment classification models, and interpreting experimental results.

title: The Strategic Roadmap for Sovereign AI - Leveraging the EU AI Act for Sustainable Competitive Advantage in European Enterprises

detail.title: The Strategic Roadmap for Sovereign AI - Leveraging the EU AI Act for Sustainable Competitive Advantage in European Enterprises
detail.abstract:
The rapid proliferation of generative Artificial Intelligence presents a critical strategic paradox for European enterprises: While the operational necessity of Large Language Models is undeniable, the reliance on US-based hyperscale infrastructure creates significant conflicts with the emerging mandates of the EU AI Act (2024). This thesis investigates the economics and architectural viability of Sovereign AI as a mechanism to resolve this tension. Adopting a design science approach, the thesis constructs a risk-adjusted Total Cost of Ownership model to evaluate two distinct architectural scenarios: The industry-standard hyperscale default and a proposed sovereign hybrid architecture, meaning isolating sensitive data within hardware-based enclaves while leveraging public clouds for elasticity.

The quantitative analysis identifies a “sovereignty tax” of approximately 25% for confidential computing architectures, driven primarily by the overhead of Trusted Execution Environments and Hardware Security Modules. However, when adjusted for regulatory liability and data breach risk, the hyperscale default scenario demonstrates a long-term cost burden 2,46 times higher than the sovereign alternative. The thesis concludes that for high-assurance workloads the sovereign hybrid architecture optimizes the net strategic value. It concludes in a four-phase roadmap, providing IT leadership with a framework to transition from regulatory dependence to a sustainable, risk-resilient AI posture.

title: When Severity and Exploitation Signals Diverge: A Cross-Sectional Study of CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities

detail.abstract: Vulnerability-management programmes frequently use technical-severity thresholds even though severity, exploitation probability, confirmed exploitation, and response context are distinct signals. This study examines every CVE added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (CISA KEV) Catalog during 18-24 August 2026 (n=9), the last complete seven-day interval preceding the official 25 August catalog snapshot. For each vulnerability, the study records CVSS v3.1 Base severity, the EPSS probability available at data collection, CISA-ADP SSVC decision points, CVE publication date, and KEV addition date. Eight of nine vulnerabilities (88.9%) had CVSS v3.1 Base scores in the Critical range (>=9.0); CVE-2026-73570 had a score of 8.9 despite confirmed exploitation. EPSS probabilities ranged from 1.506% to 72.695%, a 48.3-fold spread, with a median of 10.431%. Illustrative current-score EPSS thresholds of 5%, 10%, and 20% retained 66.7%, 55.6%, and 33.3% of this known-exploited cohort, respectively. All nine records were marked “Exploitation: active” and “Technical Impact: total” in CISA-ADP SSVC data, while two were “Automatable: no.” The elapsed time between CVE publication and KEV addition ranged from 1 to 216 days (median 12 days). These descriptive findings show that technical severity, exploitation forecasts, confirmed exploitation, and exploit automation are non interchangeable. The study does not estimate predictive performance outside the KEV-selected cohort. Its operational implication is narrower: vulnerability prioritisation systems should preserve the semantics, timestamps, and provenance of distinct signals rather than treating any single threshold or synthetic score as a substitute for confirmed exploitation and local context.

title: The Limits of AI-Mediated Decision Systems: Strategic Manipulation and Endogenous Reliance
affiliations: and National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: The Limits of AI-Mediated Decision Systems: Strategic Manipulation and Endogenous Reliance
detail.abstract: Governing decision systems vulnerable to manipulation by the agents they evaluate is a longstanding challenge. Shared AI-mediated channels, however, introduce a dynamic feedback typically absent from standard incentive-design frameworks: downstream reliance raises the return to manipulation, while manipulation degrades channel performance and subsequently weakens reliance. We develop a sender-receiver population model to study how this feedback shapes system performance and governance. In the model, senders choose whether to manipulate inputs, and receivers whether to rely on channel outputs. We show how this interaction creates a self-limiting dynamic. By attracting additional reliance, a well-performing channel can generate incentives that prevent it from realizing its full technological potential. In high-stakes environments in particular, equilibrium leaves receivers indifferent between relying on the channel and taking their outside option. Expanding reach need not expand effective use and can instead lower the equilibrium reliance rate. Governance therefore exhibits a locally all-or-nothing logic: below a critical threshold, stronger detection raises the equilibrium share of manipulators without improving delivered value. We further show that an interior level of algorithmic noise uniquely maximizes both equilibrium system effectiveness and aggregate welfare. Noise can thus serve as a governance instrument, as noisy honesty may outperform manipulable precision. Overall, our work highlights that sustaining progress in AI-mediated decision systems requires accounting for the joint endogeneity of manipulation and downstream reliance throughout system design, deployment, and oversight.

title: Attunement Costs: How Interaction Locks Users into Specific LLMs
affiliations: , New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business and TUM School of Management,Technical University of Munich

detail.title: Attunement Costs: How Interaction Locks Users into Specific LLMs
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) present near-identical conversational interfaces that impose minimal upfront learning costs. Traditional accounts of switching costs would therefore predict that users switch freely toward better-performing or cheaper alternatives. While users experiment with alternative models, they remain attached to specific models, even when objectively superior or cheaper options are available. This pattern is not readily explained by status quo bias, habit, or inertia, which predict that users would not switch in the first place. We argue that this reflects a novel form of switching cost-attunement costs-rooted in the interaction paradigm of LLM-enabled software, which offers three affordances: natural language intent articulation, probabilistic high-dimensional generativity, and discursive output engagement. These affordances shift the responsibility for effective interaction from developers, who predefine interfaces to guide interaction in traditional software, to users, who must acquire interaction-based knowledge. This knowledge follows a distinctive learning trajectory and transfers imperfectly across LLMs. Because it is tacit and concealed behind nearidentical user interfaces, its limited transferability cannot be anticipated ex ante. Attunement costs therefore manifest ex post, as degraded performance following a switch and can lead users to revert to the incumbent model. We empirically test a necessary condition of this theory by submitting 50 HumanEval coding tasks, each in four prompt variants reflecting relevant prompting techniques, to 46 LLMs (9,200 prompt-model combinations). While aggregate effects are modest, we find substantial model-level heterogeneity: prompting techniques that improve one model's performance degrade another's, with little cross-model agreement on the optimal technique. These findings are consistent with the proposed model specificity of interaction-based knowledge. The theory extends affordance-based accounts of humancomputer interaction, introduces attunement costs as a novel form of procedural switching cost, and offers a demand-side boundary condition for debates on LLM market structure and competition-a question of growing consequence as LLMs become embedded across an expanding range of private and professional technologies.

title: FinTech Integration in Cross-Border Payments: Interoperability, Risk Management, and the Transformation of Payment Infrastructure

detail.title: FinTech Integration in Cross-Border Payments: Interoperability, Risk Management, and the Transformation of Payment Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it did not involve human participants or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how the integration of FinTech platforms is transforming cross-border payment infrastructure and evaluates the implications for efficiency, interoperability, and financial risk management. Despite the scale of international payment flows, cross-border transactions continue to face high costs, fragmented infrastructures, multiple intermediaries, and complex compliance requirements.

The study applies a qualitative analytical approach based on industry data, institutional reports, payment infrastructure developments, and the XTransfer–Currencycloud case. Particular attention is given to API-based integration, ISO 20022, SWIFT infrastructure, automated compliance mechanisms, and the potential role of central bank digital currencies.

The analysis shows that FinTech integration can reduce technical and operational fragmentation without requiring the complete replacement of traditional banking infrastructure. APIs enable faster connectivity between financial institutions and specialized payment providers, while standardized messaging improves interoperability and supports more effective transaction processing and monitoring. At the same time, greater automation increases the importance of integrated AML, KYC, sanctions-screening, fraud-prevention, and transaction-monitoring systems.

The paper concludes that the future development of cross-border payments is likely to depend on interoperability between banks, FinTech platforms, standardized messaging systems, compliance technologies, and new forms of digital money rather than on a single technological solution.

title:
ICANN in the Age of AI 
Internet Identifiers, Agentic Systems, and the Next Policy Agenda

detail.title:
ICANN in the Age of AI 
Internet Identifiers, Agentic Systems, and the Next Policy Agenda
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence does not expand ICANN’s mission, but it is changing the environment in which ICANN coordinates the Internet’s unique identifier systems. AI systems increasingly interpret, generate, classify, recommend, secure, and misuse domain names and email addresses. They also mediate multilingual access, influence evidence used in abuse mitigation, support autonomous agents, and participate in multistakeholder deliberation.

Drawing on ICANN’s Bylaws, Board and organizational materials, community statements, public comments, technical proposals, and eleven public mailing-list archives, this paper examines how these developments intersect with ICANN’s existing responsibilities. The archive study reviewed 21,144 messages published between 1 August 2022 and 18 August 2026. It identified 148 messages containing explicit AI-related terminology, an aggregate salience rate of 0.70 percent. The rate reached 1.83 percent during the partial 2026 period, while five sampled GNSO policy channels recorded a combined rate of approximately 0.13 percent. The evidence indicates increasing but concentrated attention, with community interest developing faster than sustained policy engagement.

The paper organizes the intersection between AI and Internet identifiers into five domains: identifier integrity, abuse at machine speed, agent identity and accountability, multistakeholder integrity, and inclusive and universal access. It maps these domains to existing ICANN institutions and policy instruments and proposes a time-limited scoping process to distinguish matters requiring policy development from those better addressed through technical research, implementation guidance, contractual mechanisms, or community-process rules.

The analysis also explains why ICANN matters to the AI ecosystem. As AI systems become persistent users and intermediaries of Internet identifiers, their developers and providers acquire practical interests in Universal Acceptance, authoritative data, DNS abuse policy, agent identity, impersonation, and domain reputation. Effective governance will increasingly require sustained, geographically diverse, and accountable participation by the stakeholders building and operating these systems.

title: Closed-Loop Smart Microneedle Array for Predictive Glycemic Management: In-Silico Evaluation of Model Predictive Control under Physiological Disturbances and Parameter Uncertainty
affiliations: Al-Zaytoonah University of Jordan

detail.title: Closed-Loop Smart Microneedle Array for Predictive Glycemic Management: In-Silico Evaluation of Model Predictive Control under Physiological Disturbances and Parameter Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Background and objective: Continuous glucose monitoring and automated insulin delivery require control strategies that can accommodate sensor delay, physiologic disturbances, and uncertainty in transdermal transport. Microneedle arrays offer a minimally invasive route for interstitial sensing and controlled drug delivery. This in-silico study evaluates a closed-loop smart microneedle framework in which a model predictive controller (MPC) governs transdermal insulin flux under physiological disturbances and parameter uncertainty. Methods: The simulation couples a Fick-type microneedle diffusion model with a fixed 15-minute blood-to-interstitial-glucose lag. The MPC uses a 60-minute prediction horizon and 30-minute control horizon, with Q=1.0 and R=0.05 and a safety rule that suspends insulin delivery when interstitial glucose falls below 85 mg/dL. Disturbance scenarios include a 50-g unannounced carbohydrate load, moderate exercise, and stressrelated glucose elevation. Robustness was assessed using 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations with variation in skin thickness (±20%), diffusion coefficient (±15%), and lag (±5 min). Results: In the nominal hyperglycemia scenario (280 mg/dL), peak simulated transdermal insulin flux occurred at 55 minutes, and glucose returned to the 100 mg/dL target within 155 minutes without overshoot. Across the 24-hour multi-disturbance simulation, time in range (70-180 mg/dL) was 82% ± 3.2%, with no simulated time below 54 mg/dL. In the sensitivity analysis, 92.7% of runs maintained time in range above 78%, indicating relative robustness to the modeled parameter variation. Conclusions: The findings support the computational feasibility of combining predictive control with a smart microneedle delivery model for minimally invasive closed-loop glycemic regulation. The results remain in-silico and should not be interpreted as clinical equivalence to commercial automated insulindelivery systems. Experimental validation, complete controller reproducibility, sensor-noise characterization, and in-vivo testing are required before translational claims can be made.

title: AI Agents as Governance Actors in Data Trusts – A Normative and Design Framework
affiliations: University of Koblenz, , University of Koblenz and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: AI Agents as Governance Actors in Data Trusts – A Normative and Design Framework

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been supported by the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFTR), Germany, under Research Grant No. 16DHBKI039, and Research Grant No. 16DTM218 as part of the NextGenerationEU program of the European Union.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik, September 2025, Münster, Germany

detail.abstract: Data trusts have emerged as structured mechanisms to ensure responsible data stewardship grounded in fiduciary duties, transparent oversight, and user-centered governance. Meanwhile, recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) transform Information Systems by automating decisions and enabling novel data-driven applications while raising ethical, security, and trust challenges. This paper proposes a design theory that unifies fiduciary principles, institutional trust, and AI ethics to guide the integration of AI into data trusts. We introduce four design principles: fiduciary alignment, traceability and accountability, transparent explainability, and autonomy-preserving oversight. These principles protect the beneficiaries' interests and the owner's rights, mitigate opacity and conflicts of interest, and maintain robust human supervision. The framework contributes to emerging governance approaches that consider fairness, trustworthiness, and societal acceptance of AI-driven data ecosystems. We conclude with recommendations for empirical validation and sector-specific adaptations to ensure responsible AI use for the common good.

title: No Single Gate: Distributed AI Governance in Ghana's 2026 Financial-Sector Cyber Directive, and Implications for Digital Product Teams

detail.title: No Single Gate: Distributed AI Governance in Ghana's 2026 Financial-Sector Cyber Directive, and Implications for Digital Product Teams

detail.abstract: In March 2026, the Bank of Ghana revised its Cyber and Information Security Directive (CISD) and built artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) governance obligations into at least six distinct locations across the document, rather than concentrating them in a single AIspecific clause: board-level AI literacy, contractual due diligence for AI and algorithmic service providers, a dedicated Digital Innovations part, a standalone part on cyber and information security requirements for AI systems, AI/ML-specific technical testing, and a dedicated annexure of AI/ML governance and control guidelines. This exceeds what the directive gives its other major cross-cutting priorities, including third-party risk, cloud computing, and access control. One month later, the United States' banking agencies revised their own foundational model risk guidance and explicitly excluded generative and agentic AI from its scope, deferring the question to future rulemaking (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System et al., 2026). This paper uses that contrast, and the wider literature on AI governance's uneasy inheritance from model risk management (Kurshan et al., 2020; Vukovic et al., 2025), to argue that CISD 2026's distributed design has a specific, underexamined consequence for Ghana's digital product organisations: a single AI governance owner or a late compliance sign-off cannot satisfy a framework built this way. The argument has sharpened further since the directive's release: in March 2026, MTN Ghana's mobile money business was structurally separated into a distinct, separately licensed entity, meaning product teams building on top of it must now coordinate across a genuine corporate boundary. A composite illustrative case shows what those costs when discovered late. The paper closes with a practical checklist and an agenda for empirical research.

title:
Structural Reform in Digital Justice: Document Implementation Systems as Vectors for Pre-Filing Integrity 
Shifting from Reactive Intake Correction to Preventive Procedural Automation in U.S. Electronic Courts and Federal Agencies
affiliations: Florida International University

detail.title:
Structural Reform in Digital Justice: Document Implementation Systems as Vectors for Pre-Filing Integrity 
Shifting from Reactive Intake Correction to Preventive Procedural Automation in U.S. Electronic Courts and Federal Agencies
detail.abstract: The wholesale transition of the United States legal system to electronic filing (e-filing) infrastructures has achieved unprecedented scale in document transmission, yet it has simultaneously exposed a critical operational vulnerability: the systemic lack of standardized quality control during pre-filing document preparation. While digital portals efficiently route files, they function as passive conduits, unable to rectify internal data incongruences, missing mandatory exhibits, or structural disorganization originating within law firms. This structural gap generates a massive volume of preventable administrative friction-manifesting as clerk correction queues in state courts and Requests for Evidence (RFEs) in federal agencies like USCIS. This comprehensive white paper introduces the Procedural Integrity Framework (PIF), a preventive document implementation system designed to restructure law firm intake. By replacing fragmented, subjective reviews with automated schema mapping, bidirectional cross-field auditing, and rigid pre-submission readiness protocols, this model shifts the paradigm from reactive error correction to preventive procedural governance, thereby enhancing institutional efficiency and safeguarding functional access to justice.

detail.abstract: This study examines customer satisfaction towards Darkarta, a story-driven adventure game developed by Tuttifrutti Interactive. The study aims to understand players’ perceptions of the game, including gameplay experience, graphics, storyline, usability, entertainment value, and overall satisfaction. Primary data were collected from users of the game through a structured questionnaire, while secondary information was obtained from relevant sources. The study uses descriptive analysis to evaluate customer responses and identify the factors that influence satisfaction. The findings provide insights into player preferences and their perceptions of the game’s features and overall experience. The study also identifies areas where improvements can be made to enhance user satisfaction and strengthen the game’s market appeal. The research may be useful for game developers and digital entertainment companies in understanding customer expectations and improving future game development and marketing strategies.

title: Who Should Control AI Reasoning? Adaptive Reasoning versus Consumer Choice in GenAI Platforms
affiliations: , Northwestern Polytechnical University, MBS School of Business and Xidian University

detail.title: Who Should Control AI Reasoning? Adaptive Reasoning versus Consumer Choice in GenAI Platforms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conffict of interest was reported by the author(s).
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [grant number 72572129].

detail.abstract: The rapid commercialization of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has accelerated the emergence of a token-based service economy. In this economy, a new service-design question arises: who should control a GenAI system's reasoning depth-the platform or the user? We study this question using a game-theoretic model in which task requests differ in complexity and consumers differ in their ability to extract value from reasoning outputs. The platform can adopt an adaptive reasoning strategy, under which it determines reasoning depth according to task complexity, or a menu-based reasoning strategy, under which consumers choose reasoning depth. We also consider over-reasoning value, which captures the additional value generated when deep reasoning is applied to a low-complexity task. Our results yield three main insights. First, reasoning control changes how market composition translates into token pricing: as high-complexity tasks become more prevalent, the optimal token price decreases under adaptive reasoning but increases under menu-based reasoning. Second, greater over-reasoning value does not necessarily make consumer choice more attractive; its effect on the preferred control strategy is governed by nonlinear boundaries jointly determined by market structure and the over-reasoning value. Third, when overreasoning value is moderate, the optimal strategy exhibits two reversals as high-complexity tasks become more prevalent: from adaptive reasoning to menu-based reasoning, back to adaptive reasoning, and eventually to profit equivalence. These findings show that neither greater task complexity nor overreasoning value implies a one-way shift toward platform control or consumer choice, and highlight the importance of jointly designing reasoning control and token pricing in GenAI services.

title: Answerability Architecture for Corrigible AI Interaction: Corrigible Continuation without a Self
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Answerability Architecture for Corrigible AI Interaction: Corrigible Continuation without a Self

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This article develops an interactional model of corrigible artificial intelligence without attributing a self, conscience, remorse, or moral interiority to the system. Large language models can apologize, hedge, revise, cite, refuse, and self-critique, yet these behaviors may remain fluent continuation unless correction has a binding pathway. The article proposes answerability architecture as a design and governance layer for corrigible AI interaction, organized in three nested levels. First, core answerability uses contact gates to test claim status, evidence, uncertainty, falsifiers, correction warrant, burden, risk, trace, and escalation so that warranted correction can change what happens next. Second, the agentic extension moves the unit of corrigibility from isolated answers to trajectories involving authorization, reversibility, memory, handoffs, execution, monitoring, and repair. Third, future-system implications extend the same requirement to goals, generated subgoals, progress proxies, bounded autonomy, verification capacity, corrective independence, and legitimate stopping. The model distinguishes prompted corrigibility, where users ask a model to be more careful, from architectural corrigibility, where correction is distributed across system instructions, verification tools, interface design, evaluation, human workflow, and institutional responsibility. It also requires selective revision: warranted correction should bind, unsupported correction should be resisted, and unclear correction should trigger verification. The central claim is simple: AI does not need a self to be made more correctable. It needs architectures in which evidence, uncertainty, consequence, and accountable human judgment can change what happens next.

detail.abstract: A prior paper specified the Hand-Off Readiness Score as a formative index of the condition of an IT project phase transition, defined six constitutive dimensions-artefact completeness, rationale retention, traceability continuity, receiver comprehension, decision-authority clarity, and residual-ambiguity disclosure-and set out a ten-step validation roadmap of which Steps 1 and 4 were completed. This paper executes Step 2. It derives forty-eight candidate items, eight per dimension, from the constitutive definitions and from the content categories treated as mandatory in the clinical structured hand-off literature, and it pre-specifies the content-validity assessment and cognitive pretest that constitute Steps 3 and 5. Three item-writing commitments follow from the formative specification and are argued rather than assumed. Items are classified by evidence type as artefact-verifiable, receiver-judgement, or receiver-demonstration, and each dimension is required to carry a minimum proportion of items that are not matters of opinion, because a receiver-scored instrument resting wholly on receiver judgement measures disposition rather than boundary condition. Items are written to sample the full breadth of their dimension rather than to correlate with one another, since in a formative index redundancy is a defect rather than a virtue. And item retention rules are stated in advance, including the rule that a dimension falling below four surviving items triggers re-derivation of the construct rather than acceptance of a thinner index, because deleting a formative indicator alters the construct instead of merely estimating it less precisely. The paper specifies panel composition, the I-CVI, S-CVI/Ave, modified kappa, and content-validity-ratio thresholds to be applied, the two-round Delphi procedure, the think-aloud pretest protocol, and the conditions under which the item bank would be judged to have failed. No item was administered to any respondent and no validity claim is made; the bank is published in advance of testing so that the decision rules cannot be revised after the results are seen.

title: The Retraction without a Reason
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Retraction without a Reason

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or non-financial competing interests relevant to this article.

detail.abstract: A retraction notice is the journal's public justification for withdrawing confidence from a published work. When that notice says only that concerns arose, integrity was questioned, peer review was compromised, or the publisher lost confidence, it announces an outcome while concealing the reasoning needed to understand it. The result is not neutrality. It transfers uncertainty from the institution that possesses the record to readers, authors and researchers who do not. It also collapses crucial distinctions among honest error, article unreliability, publication-process failure, unresolved allegation and proven misconduct. This article argues that vague retraction notices are an ethical failure of editorial accountability and a direct contradiction of the disclosure culture that journals impose on authors. The reader's 'right to know' is framed precisely: it is a compelling publication-ethics duty and a human-rights-informed principle, not a universally enforceable private-law claim against every journal. Privacy, confidentiality, defamation risk and active investigations may justify limited redaction, but they do not justify unexplained opacity. A legally responsible notice can state verified facts, attribute findings, separate reliability from culpability, identify withheld categories and commit to updates. The article proposes a Reader-First Retraction Notice Standard and calls for retrospective correction of notices that do not explain what failed, why the article became unreliable, who decided, what process was used, and what remains unresolved. Retraction without an explanation is editorial power without public reasons.

title: When Efficiency Becomes a Driver of Strategic Fragility

detail.title: When Efficiency Becomes a Driver of Strategic Fragility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced the study does exist.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received.

detail.abstract: Efficiency is widely treated as a primary driver of organisational performance. This paper challenges that premise by specifying the conditions under which efficiency systematically erodes adaptability and undermines viability. It develops the concept of maladaptive efficiency as a regime-dependent mechanism operating under conditions of increasing environmental dynamism (ΔE↑) and temporal compression (t↓). Building on and extending research on organisational learning, dynamic capabilities, and path dependence, the analysis shows that efficiency-oriented configurations-through specialisation, structural alignment, and the reinforcement of established routinesendogenously reduce adaptive capacity (ΔC) over time. While such configurations enhance performance under stable or moderately dynamic conditions, they become structurally misaligned under high-dynamic regime conditions, where discontinuous and ongoing transformation exceeds the adaptive logic on which these configurations were built. The paper develops a causal mechanism in which strategic performance is governed by the interaction of environmental dynamism (ΔE), adaptive capacity (ΔC), and time (t). As decision cycles compress, viability depends on the system's ability to match the rate of external change with the rate of internal adaptation. Where the latter persistently falls short, a cumulative mismatch emerges, narrowing the viable strategic space and potentially leading to threshold effects and irreversible loss of adaptability. By formalising this relationship, the study advances a distinct theoretical contribution: efficiency is not merely subject to diminishing returns but can function as an endogenous constraint on adaptation. This reframing moves beyond established trade-off perspectives and provides a mechanism-based account of when and why efficiency transforms from a source of advantage into a driver of strategic fragility under high-dynamic conditions.

title: Data Driven Compliance: A SBR Solution for Regulated Entities
affiliations: Commission de Surveillance Du Secteur Financier

detail.title: Data Driven Compliance: A SBR Solution for Regulated Entities

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: EU financial regulation obliges supervised entities to report transaction-level, position-level and portfolio-level data at a granularity unmatched in any other regulatory domain. National Competent Authorities (NCAs) have begun converting these flows into Data-Driven Supervision (DDS): reproducible indicators, composite risk scores and triage pathways that allocate scarce supervisory capacity where risk concentrates (Gentilini, 2026a). DDS contributes in an efficient manner to address the fundamental needs of efficient, convergent and consistent supervision, within an architecture that combines a centralised, collegial layer for risk identification and metric design with decentralised, proximity-based application at NCA level (Gentilini, 2026b). This paper argues that the same data, the same indicator logic and the same scoring methodology can — and should — be deployed symmetrically by the entities themselves, as Data-Driven Compliance (DDC): an internal control discipline in which firms compute, monitor and remediate the very indicators their supervisors compute about them. DDC converts regulatory reporting from a terminal cost into a source of compliance assurance, lowers the cost of evidencing compliance, and creates the informational basis for a structured dialogue between entities and NCAs over which data and indicators are fit for purpose. Drawing on case studies across AIFMD, EMIR, MiFIR, MMFR and SFTR reporting — anchored in ESMA’s Data Quality Engagement Framework for the provision of data and follow-up on data quality issues — the paper formalises the DDC construct mathematically and concludes with a single actionable recommendation: ESMA should adopt dedicated Guidelines under Article 16 of its founding Regulation making it mandatory for NCAs to require supervised entities to develop and regularly use the indicator-based controls that constitute ESMA’s Data Quality Engagement Framework, to monitor their outcomes and resolve the issues they flag, and — only where issues were flagged — to report annually to their NCA on the issues identified and their resolution. The proposal is framed as simplification and burden reduction, not as new substantive obligation.

title: International Collaboration is not a Paper Mill
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: International Collaboration is not a Paper Mill
detail.abstract: The phrase ‘paper mill’ does not describe an unusual co-authorship pattern. It describes organised production, sale or manipulation of manuscripts, authorship, peer review, citations or research content. International co-authorship, repeated collaboration, multiple affiliations, disciplinary breadth and high productivity can justify a question in context; none establishes that definition. This distinction has become urgent in post-publication criticism because a globally searchable label can precede access to underlying data, author evidence, institutional inquiry and any adjudicated finding. PubPeer’s current rules require publicly verifiable information, prohibit misconduct allegations, acknowledge that comments are not scientifically reviewed, and provide no warranty of truth. Those positions cannot be reconciled with a public paper-mill label based only on network appearance. The relevant research literature supports screening, not guilt by association: one study that linked publications to a known mill relied on marketplace offers and multiple bibliographic matches, and expressly stated that suspicious collaboration is not itself misconduct. A separate network-detection study withheld identified researchers because false positives presented out of context could damage academic reputations. This article therefore calls for a categorical moderation rule: collaboration metadata may trigger confidential, paper-specific review, but may never carry a public paper-mill accusation. Any such claim must identify reproducible evidence tied to manufacture, sale, fabricated content, manipulated authorship or publication-process interference; test innocent explanations; provide notice and a meaningful response procedure; undergo independent review; and remain correctable and appealable. Until those safeguards exist, PubPeer comments should be treated only as unverified complaints, never as findings.

title: Corporate Roche Limit
affiliations: National Chiao Tung University and National Taiwan University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Corporate Roche Limit
detail.abstract: How much operating scale is sufficient for a firm to survive under competitive pressure? We introduce the Corporate Roche Limit, a firm-specific survival threshold that identifies the minimum revenue required to keep the probability of business failure below a specified level over a finite horizon. The model combines firm scale and product similarity in a boundary-crossing framework, predicting that greater revenue reduces operating-distress risk, whereas greater product similarity raises the operating scale required for survival. Using Taiwanese firm data from 2002 to 2025, we find a pronounced nonlinear relationship between revenue and business failure. The estimated Corporate Roche Limit is approximately NT$262 million for firms with low product similarity and NT$556 million for firms with high product similarity. Model calibration closely matches observed failure rates. The findings provide a new framework for understanding firm survival and the strategic value of product differentiation.

title: Overestimated Local Wisdom: Managers Misread Villagers Across the Green Peafowl's Range
affiliations: Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing University and Chinese Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Overestimated Local Wisdom: Managers Misread Villagers Across the Green Peafowl's Range
detail.abstract: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) is widely endorsed in conservation policy, yet rarely enters actual decisions. Is this because TEK is disappearing from communities, or because policies cannot accommodate it? We tested a third possibility: the frontline managers who implement any integration may misread the communities they work with. Across the entire Chinese range of the green peafowl (Pavo muticus), an endangered flagship living mostly outside protected areas, we conducted questionnaire surveys of villagers and frontline managers. Our findings showed that villagers' TEK promoted conservation behaviour almost entirely by shaping cost-benefit judgements, not willingness. Managers failed to grasp this logic where they could not reliably judge how villagers weigh costs and benefits, and assumed that knowledge directly generates willingness and behaviour. The more a manager overestimated villagers' TEK, the more difficult they perceived their grassroots work, especially inside nature reserves. This study identifies the implementing layer as an overlooked breakpoint, and suggests that bringing TEK into economic incentive structures may help bridge the last mile of TEK application.

title: Procuring Sovereignty: Public Authority under the EU Cloud and AI Act

detail.title: Procuring Sovereignty: Public Authority under the EU Cloud and AI Act
detail.abstract: The European Commission's June 2026 proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) is the Union's most ambitious attempt to translate digital sovereignty into operative law. This article argues that the proposal is significant but structurally incomplete. CADA builds a sophisticated supply-side framework: cloud providers are classified against graduated Union assurance levels; higher levels depend on third-party assessment; contracting authorities must procure at the level indicated by risk assessment; and the proposal expressly addresses extraterritorial access, service disruption and vendor dependency. Yet the responsible public institution is constituted principally as a purchaser of qualified services, not as an administrator that must remain capable of discharging public-law duties through those services. The article develops this distinction between supplier assurance and retained operational control. It examines the proposal's cumulative legal basis under Articles 114 and 173(3) TFEU, its accommodation of Article 4(2) TEU, and its reliance on private assurance and adequacy mechanisms. It then shows why Articles 41 and 47 of the Charter expose a demand-side gap concerning reasons, evidence, correction, intervention, continuity and exit. The proposed complement is not a new constitutional settlement, but procurement and governance duties preserving non-delegable public responsibility throughout the lifecycle of digitally mediated public functions.

title: When Does History Start Matter? Model-specific Sensitivity and Global Robustness in Retail Forecast Evaluation

detail.title: When Does History Start Matter? Model-specific Sensitivity and Global Robustness in Retail Forecast Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available retail datasets and does not involve human participants or patient data.

detail.abstract: Retail forecasting pipelines must decide where a product-store history begins. A common convention is to remove leading zero sales and start a series at its first positive observation, but such zeros may reflect genuine active periods rather than pre-availability. We study how this history-start convention changes forecast evaluation while holding the target observation fixed. Using Visuelle 2.0 and FreshRetailNet-50K, we compare a lifecycle-aligned or stock-grounded history with a first-positive-trimmed history across nine canonical statistical forecasting methods. In Visuelle, the affected subset is rare (262 of 106,850 series; 0.245%), yet seven of nine methods exhibit non-zero bootstrap effects and local rankings are unstable (mean Kendall's τ = 0.483), while the top method changes in only 10.6% of bootstrap samples. In FreshRetailNet-50K, 903 of 50,000 series (1.806%) contain stock-confirmed active-zero observations before first sale. Effects are smaller and heterogeneous: HistoricAverage has a positive 95% product-cluster bootstrap interval excluding zero, optimized SES has a negative interval excluding zero, and point-effect signs vary non-monotonically across evaluation origins; the corrected winner-change probability is 33.4%. In both datasets, benchmark-level scores and rankings remain largely stable, consistent with the limited prevalence of affected histories. We also show that history-dependent MASE/RMSSE denominators can reverse the apparent direction of an effect. The results motivate separating local forecast sensitivity, evaluation eligibility, benchmark propagation, and metric-normalization sensitivity when assessing preprocessing conventions.

title: Utility of the Rey 15-Item Memory Test in Compensation-Based Assessments: Prevalence of Failure and Demographic and Cognitive Correlates

detail.title: Utility of the Rey 15-Item Memory Test in Compensation-Based Assessments: Prevalence of Failure and Demographic and Cognitive Correlates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no competing interest and the author has no financial disclosure.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No formal ethics review as the report used de-identified archival data and satisfied ethics committee exemption criteria. detail.abstract:
Background The Rey 15-Item Memory Test (RMT) is a brief performance validity measure that has been used in clinical, compensation and forensic assessments. Although the test has generally demonstrated high specificity, its sensitivity to invalid performance is limited. Concerns have also been raised that performance may be influenced by demographic, educational and cognitive characteristics, potentially complicating interpretation in compensation-based assessments.
Objective This study examined the distribution of RMT scores in a large sample of people undergoing vocational assessment for compensation purposes and investigated demographic and clinical characteristics associated with RMT performance. The sensitivity and specificity of the RMT, using the traditional cut-off score of 9, were also evaluated in predicting whether claimants were working or not working at the time of assessment.
Method Archival data from 1,612 compensation claimants assessed between 2001 and 2026 were examined. Participants ranged in age from 12 to 79 years (M = 39.8, SD = 12.5). The sample included work related, motor vehicle and general liability claims. RMT performance was examined in relation to sex, age, years of schooling, English- versus non-English-speaking background, indicators of intellectual and cognitive functioning, and major injury groups.
Results RMT scores ranged from 0 to 15, with a mean of 13.1 (SD = 2.72) and a median of 15. Scores of 9 or below occurred in 11.5% of the sample. Females obtained slightly higher scores than males, although the effect was small. RMT performance was negatively associated with age and positively associated with years of schooling. Participants from non-English-speaking backgrounds obtained lower scores than those from English-speaking backgrounds, although the mean scores for both groups remained above the traditional cut-off of 9. RMT performance was also associated with several indicators of cognitive and intellectual functioning, particularly information processing speed and reading ability. No statistically significant differences were found between the brain damage, musculoskeletal and mental disorder groups examined. RMT scores also differed significantly between claimants who were working (M = 13.70, SD = 2.07) and those who were not working (M = 12.73, SD = 2.89). Using the cut-off of 9 or below to classify employment status, the RMT showed high specificity (97.2%) but poor sensitivity (11.9%), indicating that low scores were rarely obtained by working claimants but that most non-working claimants scored above the cut-off.
Conclusions The findings support the use of the RMT as a screening component within compensation-based assessments but reinforce the limitations of interpreting the traditional total recall score as a stand alone indicator of malingering or invalid performance. Most claimants performed very well, making markedly low scores relatively unusual; however, performance was associated with demographic and cognitive characteristics. The RMT also showed high specificity but low sensitivity for distinguishing working from not-working claimants, indicating that a very low score is informative but that a score above the cut-off does not exclude non-working status. RMT results should therefore be interpreted in conjunction with educational and cultural background, cognitive functioning, injury characteristics and the broader pattern of assessment findings.

detail.abstract: This working paper introduces the AMPS (Architect, Mechanism, Profiteer, Shield) framework, a diagnostic macro-governance model designed to analyse structural risk transfer loops within multidecade United Kingdom institutional failures. Over the past four decades, repetitive state and corporate failures have systematically shifted social, economic, and criminal liabilities directly onto the British public. To evaluate the efficacy of the AMPS loop, this study utilises advanced large language model (LLM)-assisted computational text-mining protocols to parse thousands of pages of official public inquiry datasets. The core verifying dataset spans five landmark UK inquiries: Grenfell Tower, Infected Blood, Brook House, Leveson, and Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust. The empirical findings reveal that these discrete institutional components coalesce into a self-reinforcing, non-linear Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) that conceals systemic deviance. This paper establishes a predictable methodology for cross-sector risk assessment, offering regulatory bodies a proactive tool to flag structural vulnerabilities before catastrophic failure occurs.

Virginia Data Center Reports. Version 1.0, August 2026. Published by Zenodo, 26 August 2026. Concept DOI (all versions) 10.5281/zenodo.22116053; version 1.0 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22116054. Licensed CC BY 4.0. These are DataCite DOIs and do not resolve through a Crossref lookup.

Virginia regulates groundwater east of a highway. The Department of Environmental Quality said so in its own words in the SJ 25 study: the strip of Coastal Plain sediment lying west of Interstate 95 "is disregarded, and I-95 is treated as the approximate western edge of the VCP aquifer system." The Commonwealth drew a regulatory boundary at the same road, and regulates as though it were real.

This executive brief crosses the three deposited volumes in the Virginia Data Center Reports water series and carries the four findings that none of them makes alone. It is organised on the three functions of SJ 25: what the study establishes, what follows where the model reaches, and what is absent where it stops.

Finding 1. Across 726 entity-bearing claims in the three volumes, four subjects carrying twenty or more claims are engaged near-evenly by all three. Three of the four are places; SJ 25 is the only document. Every institution of comparable weight is owned outright by a single volume.

Finding 2. DEQ tested nine sites and none passed at three million gallons a day. Of 286 inventoried data center facilities, 257 sit outside every declared groundwater management area, and in the northern crescent the nearest facility to Interstate 95 is 12.7 kilometres away. The flow model that produced the eastern numbers runs from Stafford south.

Finding 3. Fairfax Water's two treatment plants withdrew a combined 164.0 million gallons a day in 2024, both unpermitted under the exclusion for withdrawals in existence on 1 July 1989, against Caroline County financing a 9.0 MGD Rappahannock intake carrying a fifteen-year term, no extension, and a drought curtailment ladder, because DEQ's model says the aquifer beneath it yields 60,000 gallons a day.

Finding 4. Between the October 2024 and December 2025 editions of DEQ's Annual Water Resources Report, Prince William County's reported surface water withdrawal falls from 69.74 to 2.15 million gallons a day, a 97 percent drop accounted for almost entirely by one treatment plant being relabelled into Fairfax. Corbalis WTP at 94.6 million gallons a day appears in two tables of the December 2025 report and in no locality's row of a third.

Forty-four graded endnotes, three figures, and a routing table directing the reader to the volume that answers a given question. Evidence current to 26 August 2026. Prepared entirely from public sources, including both editions of the Commonwealth's Annual Water Resources Report read against the documents themselves.

title: Redundancy or Inventory under Export Controls: When Backup Coverage cannot be Audited
affiliations: Hunan University, Hunan University and

detail.title: Redundancy or Inventory under Export Controls: When Backup Coverage cannot be Audited
detail.abstract: Firms are urged to dual-source a critical input against export controls, but a backup adds redundancy only if it escapes the controls that cut the incumbent, and whether it does cannot be audited in advance. Only operating a backup through disruptions reveals whether its redundancy is real or illusory. We recast the qualification decision as an optimal-stopping problem in which the firm learns whether the input is a chokepoint that no backup escapes, set against an irreversible take-or-pay inventory reservation. We show that the firm's central choice is which mitigation lever to run, and that the answer turns on the input's exposure. The firm reserves outright when discriminating disruptions arrive too rarely to justify a trial, and otherwise holds out for redundancy while a chokepoint looks unlikely, falling back to inventory once its belief crosses a threshold. Against an irreversible lever choice, resolving whether the input is a chokepoint selects the lever and pays every period thereafter.

title: The Generic Retraction Notice is an Integrity Failure
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Generic Retraction Notice is an Integrity Failure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or non-financial competing interests relevant to this article.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this article.

detail.abstract: A retraction notice is the journal's public justification for withdrawing confidence from a published work. When it states only that an article was withdrawn at a party's request, that concerns arose, that misconduct occurred, or that confidence was lost, it announces a verdict while concealing the case needed to understand that verdict. This article reports a reproducible screen of a Retraction Watch Database snapshot for the ten-year period 27 August 2016 to 27 August 2026. Among 47,007 records classified as retractions, 1,581 carried the database reason code for a notice with limited or no information. Those candidates involved 624 journal or source titles, 223 recorded publisher labels and 632 publisher-source pairs. These are screening results, not findings that every listed notice remains vague: the database is mutable, its reason field can incorporate outside information, and direct verification revealed both continuing opacity and important counterexamples. Verified notices show recurring failures to identify the article-specific defect, affected content, evidence, reliability consequence or allocation of responsibility. Such formulas confuse article unreliability with personal culpability, shift reputational risk onto researchers, and exempt publishers from the disclosure culture imposed on authors. The article proposes a mandatory No-Unexplained-Retraction Standard, retrospective correction of deficient notices, case-level attribution, independent appeal and machine-readable disclosure. Confidentiality may justify precise redaction; it does not justify an unexplained final verdict.

title: From the Trenches: The Human Condition for Carrying Change Forward — A Research Agenda for Leaders and Boards in the AI Transformation Era

detail.title: From the Trenches: The Human Condition for Carrying Change Forward — A Research Agenda for Leaders and Boards in the AI Transformation Era

keywords: Human Capacity to Adopt Change in Transformation

detail.abstract: Organizational transformation has had a persistently high failure rate of 70 to 80 percent by independent industry estimates and has not meaningfully improved in three decades despite the wide availability of execution and changemanagement frameworks. A growing body of scholarship and practice has converged on the view that transformation failure is fundamentally a human and organizational problem rather than a technological one (Bohanec, 2026; Kraus et al., 2022; Plekhanov, Franke, & Netland, 2022; Vial, 2019). This is a genuine advance over technology-centric accounts of failure. However, this emerging consensus still treats the organization as the unit of analysis and its people as an aggregate workforce and has not fully escaped a slide toward treating human resistance as the limiting factor, a framing a minority of scholars has challenged (Dent & Goldberg, 1999; Cieslak & Valor, 2024). This paper proposes changing the unit of analysis, from the aggregate workforce to the individual human beings within it and begins to ask two questions: what conditions are necessary to unleash the human capacity to adapt, own, and carry large-scale change forward; and how leaders might architect those conditions in practice, under real pressure. Drawing on SelfDetermination Theory, Weick's sensemaking framework, and adjacent psychological literatures, the paper argues that large-scale change disrupts these conditions by default, and the organizational-level intervention typically deployed to address this problem, often referred to as “change management”, is top-down in its communication and outside-in in its training programs, therefore cannot restore damage occurring at a human level. This phenomenon leaves an unexamined gap in both the problem's definition and its assumed solution. This paper's contribution is the construct and the questions, not the answers yet. For leaders and boards, this paper names a blind spot in their transformation strategy and execution: the individual-level conditions those programs have not yet accounted for, and offers a starting point for seeing the fuller picture, and eventually the fuller solution. Conducting primary qualitative and quantitative empirical research to explore and define the human condition, and to codify how to build it, is indeed the research agenda the author intends to pursue next as part of her doctorate studies, and an invitation to the broader field to take up in parallel.

title: Linking ESG, Social License to Operate and Local Regulatory Compliance: toward an Integrated Sustainable Mining Governance and Performance Framework in the DR Congo

detail.title: Linking ESG, Social License to Operate and Local Regulatory Compliance: toward an Integrated Sustainable Mining Governance and Performance Framework in the DR Congo
detail.abstract:
In the era of global energy transition, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) occupies a major strategic position thanks to its significant reserves of critical minerals. However, their extraction faces persistent challenges of social and environmental  impact and governance. While Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria and the Social License to Operate (SLO) have become established international approaches in extractive sustainability, their application in contexts of fragile governance like the DRC’s remains fragmented and often disconnected from local realities.

This study examines the interactions between ESG indicators, SLO, and national regulatory obligations to illuminate the determinants of sustainable mining performance. Adopting a conceptual and theoretical approach based on a structured and integrative literature review of a multidisciplinary body of literature (scientific, institutional, and normative corpora), it develops a new framework to connect ESG, Local regulatory compliance and SLO: the Integrated Sustainable Mining Governance and Performance Framework (ISMGP Framework).

The results highlight that while ESG criteria are essential levers for legitimation, their actual effectiveness depends on their local adoption and the quality of governance. The analysis reveals systemic tensions between regulatory frameworks and acceptability, particularly where laws are proposed but poorly enforced. A “Congolese paradox” is identified: the existence of a robust formal Mining Code that nevertheless struggles to generate genuine social acceptability due to implementation gaps and information asymmetries.

To address these limitations, the ISMGP Framework integrates ESG performance, local Regulatory Compliance (RC), and SLO, using the SLO score (assessment scale, e.g scale of 1 to 5 or 1 to 7) as an operational viability coefficient that conditions formal technical performance (ESG + RC). Consequently, a deficit in social trust can transform a technically compliant project into a failed asset. Finally, the study outlines paths for future empirical and operationalization validation in the DRC mining projects to calibrate indicators and develop real-time performance monitoring tools, positioning the ISMGP as a conceptual, heuristic, governance-oriented decision-support architecture for fragile institutional contexts.

However, the progress of Indian courts has been intermittent and speaks of a prolonged period of active public policy followed by periods of restraint on the part of the judiciary. The paper will analyse the regulatory framework related to the enforcement of foreign awards in India provided by Part II of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act of 1996, as well as examine the development of public policy exceptions from Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co. to ONGC v. Saw Pipes, Vijay Karia v. Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi Srl and reveal practical, procedural, and institutional problems related to the enforcement. It is emphasised in the paper that despite the decisively pro-enforcement shift in terms of legislation and judiciary throughout the years since 2015, residual ambiguity concerning the rest of the "fundamental policy of Indian law" and chronic delays at the stage of execution continue to pose challenges to India's aspiration to be recognised as an arbitration-friendly jurisdiction.

title: The Vocabulary That Convicts: A Provenance-and-Proof Audit of Accusation-Bearing Labels in Public Post-Publication Criticism

detail.title: The Vocabulary That Convicts: A Provenance-and-Proof Audit of Accusation-Bearing Labels in Public Post-Publication Criticism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial relationship with PubPeer, the websites discussed, the named authors of public sources, or the publishers cited.

detail.abstract: Post-publication criticism increasingly depends on compact labels: paper mill, authorship for sale, citation cartel, peer-review ring, predatory journal, p-hacking, HARKing, tortured phrases, fake paper and problematic publication. These words are not neutral decorations. Some describe an observable feature; others encode a hidden mechanism, transaction, intention, organized relationship, formal finding or judgment about a person. This article introduces a lexical-warrant audit: a method for testing a label’s provenance, authoritative definition, claim level, evidentiary burden and public use before it is attached to a paper or researcher. A bounded historical PubPeer corpus shows that formal misconduct words and technical descriptors were present long before many newer mechanism labels became common, while the strongest historical claim—that most comments began with such accusations—is not supported by the dataset. The problem is therefore not demonstrated numerical dominance but evidentiary compression and amplification. Public examples show a recurring drift from anomaly to signal, signal to mechanism, mechanism to headline, and headline to person-level noun. The article proposes a ten-field Label-to-Proof Protocol and recommends that PubPeer, watchdog sites, journalists, publishers and institutions prohibit bare mechanism verdicts, require object-specific evidence and alternatives, disclose adjudication status, preserve responses, and correct propagated labels. Scientific criticism deserves protection when it is precise. It loses that claim when memorable vocabulary substitutes for proof.

detail.abstract:
Daily leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) target a stated multiple of a benchmark’s one-day return, yet realized fund returns also reflect financing, expenses, tracking, pricing, and other implementation effects. Motivated by the return-ratio covariance used by Bianchi and Goldberg (2026) to close an exact arithmetic-return identity for SSO and UPRO, this report asks a narrower econometric question: what does that covariance identify about the underlying mechanism?

The central result is a non-identification theorem. In the reduced-form representation Rₜ^{ETF} = (L + δₜ)Rₜ + uₜ, the realized return ratio satisfies λₜ = L + δₜ + uₜ/Rₜ. For any sequence hₜ, the transformation δₜ ↦ δₜ + hₜ and uₜ ↦ uₜ − hₜRₜ leaves every observed fund return unchanged while generally changing the coefficient–return covariance. Return data alone therefore do not point identify benchmark-linked coefficient timing. The report also establishes weak-denominator irregularity of the ratio and derives a correlation-dependent lower bound on the latent coefficient variation required by a timing-only interpretation.

The empirical evidence is consistent with this identification boundary. In a prespecified 2022–2023 panel of eight long 2× and 3× broad-market LETFs matched to their stated S&P 500, Nasdaq-100, Dow Jones Industrial Average, and Russell 2000 benchmarks, all annualized return-ratio covariances are negative while every intercept-regression beta remains within 0.003 of its stated daily multiple. A fixed-coefficient Monte Carlo calibrated only to the observed mean target-relative residual generates covariances of the observed scale with coefficient timing ruled out by construction. Exact log-return accounting assigns 63–68% of the SSO/UPRO shortfall relative to L times benchmark log growth to daily-reset path dependence, leaving a nonstructural implementation residual. Over complete calendar years 2017–2025, the annual mean target-relative residual for six funds is strongly negatively associated with the effective federal funds rate. After normalization by extra leverage, fund-level slopes lie between −1.25 and −1.12, close to the −1 scale implied by a stylized one-for-one reference-rate financing benchmark; the relation remains under fund fixed effects, volatility control, leave-one-year-out deletion, first differences, and within-index 3×-minus-2× comparisons. These results provide mechanism-consistent evidence for rate-linked implementation costs, but not a structural financing decomposition. Exact return accounting and structural attribution are distinct: mechanism claims require convention-matched NAV, market-price, exposure, and financing measurements in addition to returns.

title: The Compliance Chasm: Structural Decoupling in Global Resource Governance

detail.title: The Compliance Chasm: Structural Decoupling in Global Resource Governance
detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of digital traceability, sustainability regulation, due diligence,
and responsible sourcing is transforming the governance of global resource systems.
Yet improved traceability and verification have not consistently produced
corresponding improvements in institutional coordination, producer participation,
governance capability, or local value retention. This paper addresses this paradox.
It introduces the Compliance Chasm as a governance framework for explaining the
structural disconnection between expanding compliance obligations and the capacities
required to translate compliance into equitable institutional and economic outcomes.
The Compliance Chasm is defined as the structural governance condition in which
expanding compliance obligations outpace the governance capacities required to
convert compliance into equitable institutional and economic outcomes.
The paper argues that this condition is not primarily a failure of technology,
regulation, or compliance implementation. Rather, it emerges where fragmented
governance architectures leave authority, coordination, capability, and value capture
unevenly distributed across public, private, and local actors. Under such conditions,
compliance systems may enhance visibility, verification, and market access while
leaving the institutional conditions required for governance transformation largely
unchanged.
Drawing on governance theory, global value chain governance, adverse incorporation,
the Design-Reality Gap, and institutional economics, the paper develops the
Compliance Chasm as an integrative conceptual framework. Its explanatory value is
examined through the Itagunmodi-Lagos gold corridor in Nigeria, a paradigmatic case
illustrating how expanding compliance expectations interact with fragmented
institutional arrangements across artisanal extraction, commercial coordination,
regulation, and downstream markets.
The paper's central contribution is to distinguish compliance achievement from
governance achievement and to reposition compliance expansion as a distinct
governance condition requiring institutional analysis. It concludes that expanding
compliance should not be interpreted as evidence of expanding governance, providing
a new analytical lens for evaluating contemporary compliance systems and the
institutional conditions required for meaningful governance transformation.

title: Proximity vs. Pooling: Design of Parcel Locker Networks with Endogenous Service Rates
affiliations: , Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, NUS and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Proximity vs. Pooling: Design of Parcel Locker Networks with Endogenous Service Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: We study the joint location and capacity design of a spatial queueing system motivated by parcel locker operations, a widely adopted solution for last-mile delivery. Unlike classical queueing systems with exogenous service rates, locker service rates depend on customer pickup behavior and are therefore endogenous to network design. This endogeneity adds the new dimension of "where to staff" to the classical staffing question of "how many to staff": should capacity be pooled over a fixed set of locations or distributed across an expanded network to improve customer proximity? This spatial dimension gives rise to a novel proximity-pooling trade-off. On the one hand, expanding the network improves customer proximity, shortens pickup times, and increases effective service rates, thereby reducing capacity requirements. On the other hand, network expansion fragments demand across locations, weakens risk pooling, and may increase the capacity needed to absorb demand fluctuations. Our asymptotic analysis establishes the necessity of network expansion for effectively managing the proximity-pooling trade-off. Although a fixed-location design preserves demand pooling, it sacrifices customer proximity and requires total capacity to grow linearly with the parcel arrival rate. In contrast, an appropriately expanding network balances these two forces and achieves sublinear capacity growth. For the non-asymptotic regime, we develop an optimization model and reformulate it as a mixed-integer second-order cone program. A case study based on Singapore's parcel locker pilot program shows that the capacity-minimizing network expands as demand increases while retaining sufficient concentration to preserve pooling benefits.

title: Are Corporate Venture Capital and R&D Complements or Substitutes? A Process View of Absorptive Capacity
affiliations: Technical University of Denmark

detail.title: Are Corporate Venture Capital and R&D Complements or Substitutes? A Process View of Absorptive Capacity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: While both corporate venture capital (CVC) and R&D are essential vehicles for innovation, the literature has largely overlooked whether and when they act as complements or substitutes in generating firm innovation outcomes. Drawing on a process view of absorptive capacity, this paper argues that the CVC-R&D relationship depends on how firms coordinate knowledge acquisition, assimilation, transformation, and exploitation. Analyzing a sample of US firms engaged in CVC or R&D activities from 1993 to 2016, this paper finds that CVC and R&D act as substitutes in generating innovation outcomes. Furthermore, this paper finds that the substitutive relationship weakens when firms use formalized and dedicated CVC structures, and it shifts toward complementarity as firms accumulate CVC investing experience. This paper contributes to the CVC-R&D relationship literature by highlighting the role of absorptive capacity process coordination, and to the organizational learning literature by showing how experiential and deliberate learning mechanisms moderate this relationship.
