detail.abstract: Algeria's expansion of irrigated agriculture in arid and hyper-arid regions can generate crop residues, manure and agri-food by-products relevant to biogas, biomethane, biochar and nutrient recovery. This paper develops a project-status-adjusted framework that separates two questions: what circular-resource outputs are implied by announced development capacity, and what quantities can be supported by current implementation evidence. A six-stage ladder moves from gross theoretical to circularly allocable potential; soil and existing uses are deducted before logistics, and standing protective vegetation is excluded except for unavoidable maintenance residues. The principal announced-capacity envelope comprises the officially documented 153,000-ha combined scale of the Baladna and BF El Djazair parent projects. A separate inclusive sensitivity reaches 154,200 ha by adding a 1,200-ha project reported in secondary sources. To avoid presenting an unknown future crop mix as a forecast, these areas are evaluated only as a standardised wheat-straw-equivalent sensitivity. Its central 153,000-ha case yields 78,506 t yr⁻¹ of logistically recoverable residue and mutually exclusive technical ceilings of 14.80 million m³ CH₄ yr⁻¹ or 24,729 t biochar yr⁻¹. The implementation-based worked example instead uses BF El Djazair's documented 1,600-ha first-wheat-harvest module and yields 821.0 t yr⁻¹, 154,739 m³ CH₄ yr⁻¹ or 258.6 t biochar yr⁻¹ in the corresponding central screens. BF is used for methodological demonstration because public sources identify both its harvested area and crop, not because it is larger or more important than Baladna. All conversion outputs are screening ceilings rather than observed production, additive products, plant designs or contractually bankable supply.

title: The Marginal Cost of Diversification
affiliations: HEC Montreal - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Marginal Cost of Diversification
detail.abstract: Diversification reduces idiosyncratic risk, but adding securities can also change a portfolio's systematic risk. We show that these two effects vanish at different rates. Under equal weighting, the marginal reduction in idiosyncratic variance declines faster than the change in systematic variance, making the latter increasingly important as portfolios get larger. In U.S. equities, nearly half of additions that reduce idiosyncratic risk increase systematic risk, and the probability that this increase outweighs the diversification benefit rises steadily with portfolio size. The results are robust to alternative factor models, weighting schemes, samples, and residual-risk definitions.

title: An Abortion Option Can Make Women More Vulnerable to Exploitation and Abandonment
affiliations: Valparaiso University School of Law

detail.title: An Abortion Option Can Make Women More Vulnerable to Exploitation and Abandonment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: This essay argues that besides the benefits and burdens usually discussed in relation to optional abortion there are often various effects that are less well considered, paradoxically including decreases in the choices available to women, as well as additional burdens on those who decide to give birth. The key datum upon which we shall deliberate is that sex no longer causes birth. Given the availability of abortion, sexual intercourse can only cause choice. It is choice that causes birth.

title: Socioeconomic level influences the early motor repertoire of infants at biological risk in a low- and middle-income country setting
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Socioeconomic level influences the early motor repertoire of infants at biological risk in a low- and middle-income country setting
detail.abstract: BackgroundEarly neurodevelopment is shaped by biological and environmental factors. Prematurity, low birth weight, and socioeconomic adversity are linked to a higher risk of developmental impairments. The General Movements Assessment (GMA) is a reliable tool for early identification of infants at neurodevelopmental risk.ObjectivesTo describe the early motor repertoire of infants followed in a neonatal follow-up clinic using the GMA and to investigate how clinical and socioeconomic factors influence motor outcomes during the first five months of life. A secondary objective was to characterize motor performance using the Motor Optimality Score–Revised (MOS-R).MethodsThis retrospective observational study included preterm and term infants at risk for developmental impairment who were followed at the University Hospital of the University of São Paulo between March 2022 and February 2025. Videos recorded from term age to five months corrected age were analyzed using Prechtl’s GMA and the MOS-R. Clinical and socioeconomic variables were examined using linear and logistic regression models.ResultsSeventy-four infants were included; 82.4% were born preterm and 73.0% had low birth weight (<2500 g). During the writhing-movements phase, 71.4% were classified as having a poor repertoire and 10.7% as cramped-synchronized. During the fidgety movements phase, 88.2% exhibited normal fidgety movements and 11.8% had absent fidgety movements. Among 45 infants assessed with the MOS-R, 75.6% had reduced motor optimality scores. Higher family income was associated with higher MOS-R scores (β = 0.00066, p = 0.039). A poor repertoire was associated with lower birth weight (OR=0.9972, p=0.026) and lower gestational age (OR=0.9371, p=0.028).ConclusionsReduced motor optimality was common despite predominantly normal fidgety movements. Family income was significantly associated with motor optimality, highlighting the importance of integrating standardized motor assessments and socioeconomic surveillance into neonatal follow-up programs.

title: Who Survives in Private Credit? The Role of Private Equity Experience
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance and Boston College - Department of Finance

detail.title: Who Survives in Private Credit? The Role of Private Equity Experience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: NA.

detail.abstract: Private credit (PC) has grown to around $1.5 trillion in assets in the U.S., yet little is known about which lenders build lasting presence and why. We document a striking lifecycle pattern: many entrants participate only briefly, and these limited-participation "Leavers" originate smaller, higher-spread loans and account for much of the private credit pricing premium. Private equity (PE) experience strongly predicts persistence: lenders with PE experience at entry are more than three times as likely to become "Stayers," and accumulated PE deal experience lowers exit hazards. Pricing dynamics also differ: spreads rise with PC experience among non-PE lenders, but this pattern largely disappears after lenders acquire PE experience. PE experience also predicts higher subsequent take-up rates, even controlling for LP capital. Among persistent lenders, PE-experienced Stayers exhibit pricing dynamics similar to banks. Overall, the evidence points to transferable PE-related capabilities as an important determinant of sustained participation in private credit.

title: Leakage-controlled Ridge–GCN fusion improves within-cohort structural-to-functional connectome mapping
affiliations: China Jiliang University, China Jiliang University, China Jiliang University, China Jiliang University and China Jiliang University

detail.title: Leakage-controlled Ridge–GCN fusion improves within-cohort structural-to-functional connectome mapping
detail.abstract: Background and Objective:Structural-to-functional connectome mapping estimates functional connectivity (FC) from structural connectivity (SC). In small multisite cohorts, it remains unclear whether a graph neural network contributes reproducible predictive information beyond a strong regularized linear mapper when every fitted quantity is confined to the training data. We tested this question within cohort and under transfer to an unseen acquisition site.Methods:We combined complete FC predictions from a multi-output Ridge mapper and a graph convolutional network (GCN) using one convex Ridge weight selected on inner-validation predictions. Imputation, scaling, target-site correction, branch configuration, early stopping, and fusion weighting were confined to each outer-training fold. Paired 90-region connectomes from 123 male participants at three Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange II sites were evaluated by nested five-fold cross-validation, five repeated partitions, participant-level stratified bootstrap inference, and leave-one-site-out testing. Prespecified equal weighting and affine stacking tested whether selection and additional fusion flexibility were beneficial.Results:Selected fusion reduced mean squared error (MSE) by 4.4% relative to nested-alpha Ridge (0.04645 versus 0.04860) and raised fold-mean subject-wise and pooled correlations from 0.55331 and 0.59677 to 0.56579 and 0.62465. Across five repeated partitions, participant-level bootstrap intervals supported all three improvements over Ridge. A matched Ridge-to-training-mean shrinkage control selected a mean Ridge weight of 0.998 and did not improve Ridge, arguing against simple shrinkage as the source of the GCN fusion gain. Selection improved subject-wise correlation over equal weighting, whereas its MSE advantage was small. Under leave-one-site-out testing, neither fusion nor the individualized Ridge mapper consistently outperformed the training-site mean FC baseline.Conclusions:Validation-selected Ridge–GCN fusion improved within-cohort SC-to-FC mapping beyond a nested-tuned linear baseline, and a matched shrinkage control did not reproduce the gain. The advantage did not transfer consistently to unseen sites. The result supports low-dimensional prediction fusion for the evaluated cohort while identifying acquisition-site generalization as its principal boundary.

title: Balanced Multimodal Learning Integrating 3D CT and Clinical Data Enhances Survival Prediction in Cirrhotic Patients
affiliations: Ajou University, Ajou University, Ajou University, Ajou University School of Medicine, Ajou University, Ajou University School of Medicine, Ajou University School of Medicine, Ajou University School of Medicine and Ajou University - Department of Software and Computer Engineering

detail.title: Balanced Multimodal Learning Integrating 3D CT and Clinical Data Enhances Survival Prediction in Cirrhotic Patients
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Accurate prediction of survival outcomes in patients with liver cirrhosis is challenging due to the complex nature of disease progression. Radiomic analysis of routinely acquired computed tomography can expose structural disease burden that laboratory-based scores do not represent, so multimodal fusion of imaging with clinical data holds promise. However, dominant modalities tend to suppress weaker ones during joint training, a phenomenon known as modality laziness, which limits the contribution of imaging. This study proposes an interpretable multimodal survival prediction framework that fuses clinical features with three-dimensional computed tomography (3D CT) imaging for time-to-event prediction in cirrhotic patients.,Methods: The framework addresses modality imbalance through auxiliary unimodal regularization with alternating adaptation. For explainability, we developed Survival Activation Maps, a gradient-free attribution method quantifying the contribution of each spatial feature to predicted risk, since gradient-based attribution is unreliable in multimodal survival models. Performance was evaluated in 3,354 patients across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)-free, liver transplantation (LT)-free, and HCC/LT-free survival using the concordance index, the integrated Brier score, and the time-dependent area under the curve, with Kaplan–Meier analysis, log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards regression on the held-out test set.,Results: The proposed framework significantly outperformed clinical-only and conventional multimodal baselines across all three outcomes (all p<0.01), with concordance indices of 0.723, 0.805, and 0.755 versus 0.706, 0.789, and 0.737 for conventional multimodal fusion, confirming modality laziness. Survival Activation Maps localized consistently to hepatic and peri-hepatic regions, and albumin and age emerged as the dominant clinical predictors, indicating that 3D CT imaging contributed substantively to survival prediction.,Conclusions: Conventional multimodal integration improved only marginally over clinical-only models, whereas explicitly counteracting modality laziness through alternating unimodal adaptation produced consistent gains and enabled the imaging encoder to contribute meaningfully. By capturing structural features that biochemical markers do not represent, the framework also outperformed four established clinical risk scores. Balanced and explainable multimodal fusion of 3D CT imaging with clinical data therefore enables more individualized risk stratification in cirrhosis than laboratory-based scores, and may identify high-risk patients whose risk is underestimated by preserved liver function tests, supporting intensified surveillance and earlier transplant evaluation.

title: Integrating Mathematical Modelling and Artificial Neural Networks to Reveal the Transmission Dynamics of Marburg Virus Disease
affiliations: Northwest University Kano, Northwest University Kano, Northwest University Kano, Taif University, Sule Lamido University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Integrating Mathematical Modelling and Artificial Neural Networks to Reveal the Transmission Dynamics of Marburg Virus Disease
detail.abstract: The Marburg virus disease MVD, or MHF (Marburg haemorrhagic fever), is an illness characterized by high mortality rate that is caused by filoviruses. MVD is transmitted through exposure to either an infected bat, an infected person, or a contaminated environment. In this research, we study a deterministic compartmental model of the dynamics of Marburg virus disease by incorporating asymptomatic, hospitalized and Deceased compartments to SEIR model. The positivity and boundedness, basic reproduction number and equilibrium points were obtained. Further, we verify the stability of the Marburg disease-free equilibrium (MDFE) and Marburg endemic equilibrium (MEE) points globally .The impacts of the model parameters was visualized using 3-D and contour plots and sensitivity analysis. Moreover, the numerical solution of the proposed model and its approximation was depicted using artificial neural network (ANN).

title: Construction of Input-Output Table and its Multipliers (2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19)

detail.title: Construction of Input-Output Table and its Multipliers (2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: In this paper, I conducted comparative analysis of the India’s Input-Output Tables (IOT) for 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2018-19 along with its multipliers with high accuracy and precision. The IOTs are constructed with seven essential sectors: Agriculture (agriculture, livestock, forestry logging, fishing, and aquaculture), Mining and Quarrying, Manufacturing, Construction, Trade and Transportation, Service Industries, and Public Administration and Defence. These sectors were mapped and aggregated per the new Supply and Use Tables’ supplementary note provided by the Central Statistical Office (CSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Government of India, who also provides the Supply and Use Tables (SUTs) data, rather than the conventional guidelines structured in Central Product Classifications (CPC) and National Industrial Classifications (NIC). I, also, took the opportunity to clearly state the process and formulation used in the creation of four different IOTs (models) based on assumptions pertaining to technology and fixed sales structures for both product-by-product and industry-by-industry categorizing the output and transaction of the intermediate consumption and final demand in the Indian economy for the mentioned financial years. The multipliers for output, income, gross value added (GVA), import, and trade and transportation margins were computed. The results of the analysis for the three IOTs (2016- 17, 2017-18, and 2018-19) modelled to output vs input vis-à-vis model used aligned with the respective year, shows no definitive pattern or trend w.r.t any given sector. Though, behaviour does not vary at large with not much difference in the slopes. I can conclude that model A (product-by-product IOT based on product technology assumption) is the best fitted IOT model for India. Though, results for other models are comparable. These results reflect the Indian economy at large for three consecutive financial years and can be applied to understand the economic structure of the Indian economy and possible macroeconomic outcomes through exogenous shocks. Given the wide applications of IOTs and multipliers in policy research analysis, this paper may be used as a readily available data source by researchers and policymakers.

title: COVID-19 & Cost Stickiness In Private Health Insurance Markets: Evidence from Australia
affiliations: University of Cape Town (UCT) - Graduate School of Business

detail.title: COVID-19 & Cost Stickiness In Private Health Insurance Markets: Evidence from Australia
detail.abstract: This paper examines the dynamics of COVID-19 pandemic and asymmetric cost behaviour in the Australian private health insurance (PHI) market. Using panel data on 44 PHIs from 2007/2008 to 2022/2023, the paper documents evidence in support of varying cost behaviors for different cost drivers under different environmental conditions. First, the paper finds sales and general administrative component of the PHIs costs to be sticky while health benefit fund costs are anti-sticky over the study period. The estimates translate into the decline of AU$279,460 in sales and general administrative costs for AU$5,816,676 decrease in total revenue. Second, the advent of the COVID-19 pandemic induces sticky health benefit fund costs while sales and general administrative costs become elastic. This equates to AU$2,374,455.434 decrease in health benefit fund costs from a revenue decline of AU$5,816,676 during the pandemic. This reflects a highly inelastic (elastic) health-related (operational) costs during the pandemic and highlights the role of the COVID-19 health emergency on cost behavior. The findings highlight the sensitivity of PHIs to resource allocation decisions when faced with uncertainties and contributes to the understanding of the dynamics of cost behavior during environmental uncertainties.

title: Mapping Sovereignty and Competition Concerns Along the Generative AI Value Chain
affiliations: Maastricht University

detail.title: Mapping Sovereignty and Competition Concerns Along the Generative AI Value Chain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No data collected.
declarations.funderStatement: Not a funded research.

detail.abstract: Competitive, technological and data advantages in the platform economy have offered leading digital firms, such as Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Apple (GAMMA), a competitive lead in the generative AI race for supremacy. Recent innovations by the large digital players, such as the 'word vectors' and 'transformers' by Google and innovative developments in graphics processing units by Nvidia, have contributed to rapid developments in the industry. Emerging champions in generative AI are either the incumbent digital gatekeepers or, if a new entrant (OpenAI), have benefited richly from the support provided by the current gatekeepers. Discernibly, a handful of digital oligarchs repeatedly influence each successive wave of innovation and design standards for the critical technological infrastructure. This contribution decodes the complex value chain of generative AI and maps how these competition concerns also qualify as digital sovereignty along the digital stack. The discussion looks at the AI infrastructural layer and self-preferencing in search. Appreciation of the underlying policy rationale of a regulatory measure can facilitate more effective implementation. The discussion maps generative AI on the competition law and Digital Market Act's regulatory landscape, and illustrates the latter's hitherto implicit sovereignty goal, alongside its more widely accepted pursuit of fairness and contestability.

title: Historical and Modern Legacies of the Centrality Gradient
affiliations: Tulane University, University of California Berkeley, Haas School of Business and

detail.title: Historical and Modern Legacies of the Centrality Gradient

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Using 873 polities spanning 3400 BCE to 1500 CE on a fixed quarter-degree grid, we estimate a centrality gradient with great-circle distance and human mobility cost, showing cells farther from the center of a historical polity were less densely populated. Cross-sections show this gradient steepens with a cell's cumulative years under rule, and a within-cell panel identifies it from plausibly exogenous border movements. As evidence of public good provision and accumulation, Roman road density declines with distance holding population fixed. Distance to the historical center still explains where modern capitals sit, but not modern population density or nighttime lights.

title: CVaR Estimation Error Bounds for Normalizing Flow Generative Models with EVT Tail-Index Analysis

detail.title: CVaR Estimation Error Bounds for Normalizing Flow Generative Models with EVT Tail-Index Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: A study on how wrong a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) estimate can be when it comes from a normalizing flow trained on financial return data. Composing a classical CVaR-Wasserstein stability bound with an extreme-value-theory rate for empirical Wasserstein convergence gives a computable error bound whose finite-sample terms shrink at rate γ(α) = min(1/2, (α-1)/α), where α is the tail index of the return distribution; the rate degrades once α falls below 2. I evaluate this bound, and a tail-restricted tightening of it, on three real return series: the S&P 500, and Bitcoin before and after the launch of CME futures. An in-sample check of either bound is guaranteed to hold by construction and is therefore not really a test, so I add a chronological out-of-sample protocol: the flow, the tail index, and every bound constant are estimated on the first 70% of each series and evaluated against the CVaR of the unseen remaining 30%. The unrestricted bound survives this test on all three assets; the tightened, tail-restricted version fails on two of three, exposing a tightness-robustness trade-off invisible to the in-sample check. I also build a flow with a learnable Student-t base: it improves both Wasserstein distance and CVaR accuracy over a Gaussian base, but its learned degrees-of-freedom parameter turns out not to identify the tail index: it tracks its initial value rather than the data. Reported alongside these results are how uncertain the tail-index estimates themselves are (two of my three assets are not resolvably above or below α = 2), a comparison against Historical Simulation and GARCH-EVT, a split-conformal error certificate, and a regulatory-style certification protocol under which pre-CME Bitcoin cannot be certified at a ±0.5 percentage-point tolerance, a result driven mainly by its volatility scale and small sample rather than its tail index alone.

title: Which Diagnoses Change How Long People Think They Will Live: Cancer against other first diagnoses in three ageing panels
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa - Department of Quantitative Health Sciences

detail.title: Which Diagnoses Change How Long People Think They Will Live: Cancer against other first diagnoses in three ageing panels
detail.abstract: A serious diagnosis is news that one will not live as long as expected. In three panels I compare first cancer diagnoses with first diagnoses of heart disease, stroke, diabetes or lung disease. Cancer lowers the stated chance of reaching a target age four to five percentage points further than the other four combined, on the survey's scale. Against what later mortality justifies, cancer delivers the largest share in every survey, and every diagnosis warranting more than cancer delivers less: American lung disease warrants 2.3 times cancer's revision and delivers 17 percent of it, against cancer's 94. Cancer's first place is a tested result in the American panel (probability 1.00) but not in the continental European one (0.72), where the runner-up's interval is too wide to rank. What reaches the belief tracks the name of the disease more closely than the danger it carries.

title: Uniform Inference for Conditional Quantile Functions under Time-Series Dependence
affiliations: Zhejiang University

detail.title: Uniform Inference for Conditional Quantile Functions under Time-Series Dependence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that I have no conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: We develop feasible uniform inference for conditional quantile functions estimated by series quantile regression from dependent time-series data. A uniform Bahadur representation linearizes the nonsmooth, growing-dimensional estimator, while a maximum-norm Gaussian coupling approximates the leading quantile-score vector under serial dependence. We provide primitive sufficient conditions for uniform linearization and feasible long-run covariance estimation, accommodating both martingale-difference and mixingale score processes. These results yield asymptotically valid uniform confidence bands at a fixed quantile and jointly over a finite quantile grid, together with a uniform specification test for parametric conditional quantile models. Monte Carlo simulations show rejection frequencies close to nominal levels and good power against nonlinear alternatives, with substantial gains from joint testing when misspecification varies across quantiles. In an application to daily U.S. equity returns, the conditional lower tail steepens as market volatility rises, and linearity is rejected in the lower tail but not at the median.

title: Verification Practice and Ethical AI Awareness as Predictors of Responsible AI Governance in Cambodian Upper Secondary Education
affiliations: , Royal University of Cambodia, Royal University of Cambodia and Royal University of Cambodia

detail.title: Verification Practice and Ethical AI Awareness as Predictors of Responsible AI Governance in Cambodian Upper Secondary Education

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This aim to enhance the Cambodian upper secondary school's critical thinking and Academic Performmance in Cambodia through the Development of Critical Cogintive Scaffold to support AI uses.
declarations.funderStatement: In Cambodia, I do this research without any finacial support. So I am looking for those can support this research.

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has created significant opportunities for personalized learning, information access, feedback, and academic support while simultaneously introducing concerns regarding misinformation, academic integrity, privacy, ethical decision-making, and human oversight. Responsible AI governance in secondary education therefore requires more than technological knowledge; it requires students to critically evaluate AI-generated information, recognize ethical responsibilities, and retain human responsibility for AI-assisted decisions. This study investigates the relationships among AI Literacy, Ethical AI Awareness, Verification Practice, Human-AI Collaboration, and AI Governance among upper-secondary students in Cambodia. A quantitative research design was employed using questionnaire data collected from 450 Grade 10-12 students in selected public upper-secondary schools. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, one-sample ttests, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for data analysis. The results showed positive mean levels across all five constructs, ranging from 3.46 to 3.64 on a five-point Likert scale. All constructs were significantly above the neutral midpoint. AI Governance was significantly correlated with AI Literacy (r = .611), Ethical AI Awareness (r = .672), Verification Practice (r = .737), and Human-AI Collaboration (r = .583), with all correlations significant at p < .001. Multiple regression demonstrated that the four predictors jointly explained 57.1% of the variance in AI Governance (R² = .571, adjusted R² = .568, F = 148.3, p < .001). Verification Practice was the strongest significant predictor (B = .553, p < .001), followed by Ethical AI Awareness (B = .254, p < .001). AI Literacy (B =-.005, p = .938) and Human-AI Collaboration (B = .031, p = .600) did not make significant unique contributions. These findings suggest that responsible AI governance should move beyond a technology-centered approach toward a humancentered model emphasizing critical verification, ethical awareness, AI literacy, and human responsibility. Based on the empirical findings, a Human-Centered AI Governance Framework is proposed for responsible AI use in Cambodian secondary education.

title: Does It Matter How We Ask? Estimating Hypothetical Bias in Households' Willingness to Accept Thermal Discomfort
affiliations: ZHAW School of Management and Law, ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences and  ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences, School of Management and Law

detail.title: Does It Matter How We Ask? Estimating Hypothetical Bias in Households' Willingness to Accept Thermal Discomfort

keywords.keywords: Hypothetical biasWillingness to acceptDiscrete choice experimentContingent valuationDemand responseField experiment

detail.abstract: Stated-preference (SP) methods are routinely used to value demand-flexibility contracts in residential energy markets, yet their external validity remains contested. We exploit a paired randomized controlled trial and survey experiment on the same households to estimate hypothetical bias in willingness to accept (WTA) thermal discomfort from heat-pump curtailment. A discrete choice experiment (DCE) and a contingent valuation method (CVM) survey were administered before and after a field experiment in which households faced real financial incentives to curtail their heat-pump electricity consumption. The resulting stated WTA values are benchmarked against the revealed WTA implied by households' actual electricity responses. Revealed WTA amounts to about CHF 200 per degree Celsius of indoor temperature reduction per day (°C-day) and exceeds the DCE-derived estimate of about CHF 17 per °C-day by roughly a factor of twelve and the baseline CVM-derived estimate of about CHF 70 per °C-day by roughly a factor of three. Stated valuations do not move closer to the revealed benchmark after households experience real curtailment, suggesting that experiential learning alone does not correct hypothetical valuations of thermal comfort loss. The findings caution against relying on SP estimates alone in demand-response program design and contribute new evidence on whether the DCE or the CVM format is less susceptible to hypothetical bias.

title: Sovereign Risk Weights, Bank Capital Floors, and Monetary Transmission
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidad Pablo de Olavide and Federal University of Goias

detail.title: Sovereign Risk Weights, Bank Capital Floors, and Monetary Transmission
detail.abstract: We study how sovereign risk weights shape monetary-policy transmission to bank credit in an emerging-market small open economy. In a New Keynesian DSGE model calibrated to Brazil, a representative bank holds long-duration government bonds and floating-rate debt indexed to the Selic rate while facing a regulatory capital floor. A monetary tightening lowers long-bond prices, generating mark-to-market losses that erode bank capital. With low sovereign risk weights, these losses reduce capital without commensurately reducing risk-weighted assets; once the floor binds, the bank contracts private credit.The central result is an activation frontier in sovereign exposure and the effective capital buffer. On its slack side, tightening has muted balance-sheet effects; on its constrained side, credit contracts sharply, by an order of magnitude more under zero than under full sovereign risk weights. Using supervisory data, a direct-securities upper bound places Brazil near the threshold, while a repo-inclusive proxy lies inside the constrained region. Selic-indexed debt attenuates the channel by reducing duration exposure. For the same cumulative disinflation, front-loaded tightening generates larger losses than gradual tightening, especially when bank portfolios are tilted toward long-duration debt.In a two-constraint extension, bank-capital stress makes the borrower collateral constraint more likely to bind and more persistent. Deleveraging, however, reduces risk-weighted assets and partially relaxes the bank floor. The constraints are complementary in the incidence and persistence of borrower collateral stress, but their interaction attenuates peak credit and output losses. The mechanism requires neither sovereign default nor risk mispricing; the sovereign risk weight remains the key policy margin.

title: Asymmetries at the core of short-term return predictability
affiliations: , SKEMA Business School and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Asymmetries at the core of short-term return predictability
detail.abstract: We study short-horizon equity return predictability using high-frequency data and show that asymmetries in the core}of the return distribution contain information about expected returns. Decomposing intramonth returns into core and tail components and distinguishing between downside and upside realizations, we define core asymmetry as the difference between typical upside and downside variation. Core asymmetry robustly predicts one-month-ahead market returns and outperforms traditional predictors at the one-month horizon. Predictability is strongest in high-stress periods, when risk-bearing constraints are likely to be tighter. As an economic interpretation, a reduced-form pricing illustration suggests how a state-dependent price of risk can amplify the return implications of downside core variation.

title: The Diminishing High-Volume Return Premium: Persistent Volume States in a Changing Market Environment
affiliations: Kangnam University and Seoul National University

detail.title: The Diminishing High-Volume Return Premium: Persistent Volume States in a Changing Market Environment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: We examine the long-run evolution of the high-volume return premium (HVRP) in U.S. equities from 1964 to 2025. The premium is statistically persistent but economically unstable: it is significantly positive in 50 of 61 reported years, yet declines markedly over time and is indistinguishable from zero in 2024–2025. This attenuation occurs long after the original Gervais, Kaniel, and Mingelgrin (2001) publication, making a simple post-publication anomaly-decay explanation incomplete. We show that the underlying relative-volume states persist even as their return implications change. The historical HV–MV return differential weakens as the price response to high-volume events becomes increasingly concentrated near the formation day, while recent low-volume states represent substantially higher absolute trading activity than historical low-volume states. Baseline trading activity also historically predicts the speed of post-event adjustment, but this separation becomes much weaker in the recent sample. Cross-sectional sorts further show that absolute turnover and dollar volume do not reproduce the HVRP, whereas changes in turnover generate a more similar return ordering. The evidence suggests that the HVRP reflects a transient relative-activity state whose return consequences depend on the trading and information environment in which it occurs. These findings are consistent with faster incorporation of trading-related information in recent markets.

title: The Cross-Section of Price Changes in Prediction Markets
affiliations: ,  and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF)

detail.title: The Cross-Section of Price Changes in Prediction Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We study cross-sectional price changes using 96,860 contracts from Kalshi, a regulated prediction market. Contracts with low YES-side market value subsequently appreciate relative to those with high market value. Recent price movements measured by one- to six-day log odds ratios (LORs) subsequently reverse. The relation between YES-side market value and subsequent price changes is stronger among contracts with wider quoted bid-ask spreads and greater price impact. Reversal is concentrated on the next day and in the contract-specific component of price changes. Despite weak comovement across official categories, three principal components explain 63% of the variation in 27 prespecified characteristic-portfolio spreads. Finally, among textually similar event pairs, a text-based classification of whether the two YES claims should move in the same or opposite directions predicts realized price comovement beyond textual similarity alone.

title: Autonomous AI Decision-Making Under Uncertainty Using Machine Learning and Reinforcement Learning

detail.title: Autonomous AI Decision-Making Under Uncertainty Using Machine Learning and Reinforcement Learning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest associated with this research or its publication. The author has no financial, personal, professional, or institutional interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study because the research was based on a literature review and conceptual analysis and did not involve human participants, animals, or the collection of personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In uncertain environments, with incomplete, dynamic or inaccurate information, autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems can play an increasingly important role, and decisions must be made in such environments. These kind of systems find application in robotics, autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, intelligent transportation, healthcare support systems and other complex systems/environments that demand continuous adaptation. Traditional machine learning methods have strong pattern recognition and prediction capabilities but can be restrictive if the autonomous agents need to make autonomous decisions in ever-changing environments. Another alternative is reinforcement learning (RL), which allows agents to learn from repeated interaction with their environments and to adapt their decision making policies to maximize the rewards that they receive on the basis of feedback (Watkins & Dayan, 1992; Kaelbling et al., 1996). Autonomous systems have also recently been equipped with additional techniques to tackle uncertainty and operational risk, such as deep reinforcement learning (Mnih et al., 2015), risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (Bellemare et al., 2017), Bayesian reinforcement learning, distributional reinforcement learning, and safe reinforcement learning (Prashanth & Fu, 2022; Kang et al., 2024). This study critically explores the potential for enhancing the autonomous decisionmaking process of AI in uncertain environments using machine learning and reinforcement learning methods. The research methodology is structured literature based analytical which is a combination of basic theories and current theories related to developing autonomous learning and decision making. The analysis suggests that, including uncertainty estimation, risk sensitivity, adaptive learning, safety constraints, and continuous environmental feedback into decision architectures would lead to more reliable decisionmaking behavior in the face of uncertainty. The study eventually concludes that, it is not a complete solution to the uncertainty with just reinforcement learning. However, a strong autonomous AI system needs to include a unified framework that leverages predictive machine learning, uncertainty modelling, risk-aware policy optimization and solid safety measures.

title: Mind the gap: linking individual adaptation decisions to global climate mitigation policy
affiliations: RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment, , , Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC) and RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment

detail.title: Mind the gap: linking individual adaptation decisions to global climate mitigation policy
detail.abstract: Adapting to climate change is a complex decision process sensitive to local contexts and contingent on global mitigation pathways. At the same time, aggregate individual economic choices have important repercussions for global climate strategies. Climate-economy models characterizing global mitigation and impacts pathways lack geographical detail and behavioral heterogeneity to represent micro-level adaptation to climate change. This paper introduces a bidirectional coupling between a climate-economy integrated assessment (RICE50+) and a regional economic agent-based model (CRAB) incorporating multiple autonomous adaptation strategies against different climate hazards. Our framework captures climate-economy interactions where changing climate conditions adversely affect local flooding and labor productivity, while location-based adaptation investments feed back into aggregate macro-level damage functions. Using detailed spatial climate impacts data under different global mitigation scenarios as well as behavioral survey data from the Netherlands and USA, we demonstrate significant regional variation in adaptation patterns, costs, and efficiency. Cost-benefit analysis reveals consistently positive but mitigation policy-dependent and country-specific returns from private adaptation. Moreover, we find that adaptation complements rather than substitutes mitigation efforts. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the results remain robust across a wide range of parameters. This coupled modeling approach provides a robust platform for evaluating climate strategies that bridge local adaptation decisions with global climate dynamics.

title: A Hybrid ODE–LSTM Framework for Demand and Inventory Optimization of Perishable Pharmaceuticals: A Proxy-Data Feasibility Study for the Kenyan Context
affiliations: Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology

detail.title: A Hybrid ODE–LSTM Framework for Demand and Inventory Optimization of Perishable Pharmaceuticals: A Proxy-Data Feasibility Study for the Kenyan Context
detail.abstract: Pharmaceutical supply chains in resource-constrained environments face high stockout rates and financial losses from drug expiration. This study develops a hybrid framework integrating an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) model of inventory depletion and deterioration with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for demand estimation, augmented with a 14-day lagged weather signal motivated by the Kenyan malaria transmission cycle. A censored-demand filter corrects stockout-masked zero-sales records prior to training. Demand and cost estimates feed a Newton-Raphson optimizer, verified against an independent grid search, computing the cost-minimizing order quantity Q* under a symmetric shortage/deterioration cost weighting. Because live Kenya Medical Supplies Authority (KEMSA) records could not be accessed, the framework was evaluated on a proxy sales dataset with a simulated weather covariate; all results are proxy-dataset findings. On a 10,073-hour held-out test set, the hybrid model achieved a 22.9% RMSE and 47.0% MAE improvement over a moving-average baseline. An ablation isolating the weather-lag signal found it negligible for RMSE (-0.15%) and modest for MAE (-9.3%), indicating the LSTM architecture and censored-demand correction account for most of the accuracy gain. A retrospective shadow simulation found a 9.7% cost reduction (annualized savings of KES 64,875 per facility) and a 98.4% reduction in simulated unmet demand, achieved at the cost of a 17.7% increase in simulated drug expiry — a genuine cost-shortage-expiry trade-off consistent with newsvendor theory, not a uniform improvement on every metric. These findings support the framework's feasibility and motivate validation on real KEMSA data before any deployment claim.

title: The Post-Notification Era: Designed Fragmentation, Algorithmic Identity, and the Path Toward Human Coherence

detail.title: The Post-Notification Era: Designed Fragmentation, Algorithmic Identity, and the Path Toward Human Coherence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no financial or personal relationships that could reasonably be seen as influencing this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not report research involving human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data. It is a conceptual and literature-based study, so formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was developed independently through The Emerging Human Lab.

detail.abstract: I developed the Post-Notification Era framework to name a transition I kept living through before I had language for it: the movement beyond reactive digital life toward intentional, coherent human agency (Smith, 2026h). Attention researchers have spent two decades documenting what happens to sustained focus under constant interruption (Mark et al., 2005; Mark, 2023; Mark et al., 2008). Communication scholars have studied how personalization narrows what a person encounters (Pariser, 2011) and how platforms convert behavior into a commercial asset (Zuboff, 2019). Developmental psychologists disagree, sometimes sharply, about what smartphones have done to adolescent loneliness (Twenge et al., 2019, 2021; Heffer et al., 2019). Creativity researchers have shown that boredom can precede certain kinds of original thought (Mann & Cadman, 2014). None of these literatures were built to talk to each other. That is the gap this paper works in. My argument is that these fields are describing facets of a single shift for which Designed Fragmentation, Human Coherence, and Sovereignty offer a shared vocabulary. I treat Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000, 2017) as the clearest existing account of what Sovereignty would require psychologically, while marking where my framework extends beyond what any single study can support.
